topic: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
parentTitle: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
title: Older people: dementia, delirium and late-life depression
blurb: Tell delirium, dementia and depression apart, use the 4AT, and follow NICE on antipsychotics in dementia.
question: Mrs Okafor, 84, has Alzheimer's disease and lives on an older adults' mental health ward. Over 2 days she has become sleepy, quiet and slow to answer, and is eating little. Staff say she is 'settling in'. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by physical illness, drugs or withdrawal. Dementia is a progressive decline in memory and other thinking skills over months to years. Depression in later life can look like dementia, with slowness and poor concentration. A person can have more than one at once: dementia is a major risk factor for delirium. Plain English: any sudden change in an older person is delirium until proved otherwise.

teach.caption: Standard teaching. Acute onset, fluctuation and inattention point to delirium.
CG103 1.2.1, 1.5.1, 1.6.1, 1.7.1. In critical care use CAM-ICU or ICDSC instead of the 4AT.

teach.h: Hypoactive delirium is the one we miss
teach.body: Hyperactive delirium is noisy: agitation and restlessness. Hypoactive delirium is quiet: the person is withdrawn, sleepy, slow to respond, moving less and eating less. NICE asks staff to be particularly vigilant for it because it is often missed or mistaken for depression, tiredness or 'settling in'. People with hypoactive delirium can still be distressed, for example by hallucinations.

head: Rule
Detail
rows: Structured assessment; psychosocial and environmental measures
Risk of harm, or severe distress from agitation, hallucinations or delusions
No clear ongoing benefit, after discussion
teach.caption: MHRA 2012: increased risk of stroke and death. Lewy body and Parkinson's disease dementia: risk of severe sensitivity reactions (1.7.4).

items.label: age is a delirium risk factor

teach.caption: CG103 1.7.4: short-term haloperidol only if de-escalation fails or is unsuitable; caution in Parkinson's and Lewy body dementia.

teach.h: Nursing care for delirium and dementia
items: Reorientate: explain where the person is, who you are and your role; clock, calendar, good lighting (CG103 1.4.4, 1.7.2).
Glasses and hearing aids in and working; involve family and carers.
Protect sleep: avoid procedures and medicine rounds during sleep hours, keep noise down.
Check for pain, constipation, retention, infection, dehydration and drugs with high anticholinergic burden (CG103 1.7.1; NG97 1.6.1-1.6.2, 1.7.1).
De-escalate first; avoid moving bed or ward where possible.

teach.body: A change over 2 days in a woman with dementia, with sleepiness, slowness and poor appetite, fits hypoactive delirium, not 'settling in'. The nurse records observations including NEWS2, completes a 4AT and escalates for medical review to look for a cause such as infection, dehydration, constipation or a new medicine. She asks the family how this compares with Mrs Okafor's usual self, keeps her glasses and hearing aid in, and documents the change.

teach.text: Quiet does not mean settled. Hypoactive delirium is often missed or labelled as depression. Also: antipsychotics are NOT first line for distress in dementia; and in Lewy body or Parkinson's disease dementia they can cause severe sensitivity reactions.

items: Delirium: acute, fluctuating, inattention; assess with the 4AT; treat the cause.
Be vigilant for hypoactive delirium: withdrawn, sleepy, slow, eating less.
Dementia distress: assess causes, psychosocial measures first; antipsychotics only for harm or severe distress, review every 6 weeks.
Depression in older age can mimic dementia; investigate reversible causes before diagnosing dementia.

summary: You can now tell delirium, dementia and depression apart, use the 4AT and spot hypoactive delirium. You can also apply NICE NG97 to antipsychotic use in dementia, including the 6-week review and the Lewy body warning.

A.q: Which tool does NICE CG103 recommend for assessing suspected delirium on a general ward?
options: The 6CIT
The 4AT
The Mini-Cog
The CAM-ICU
A.why: CG103 1.6.1 (2023): if indicators of delirium are present, a competent practitioner should assess using the 4AT.

whyNot.0: The 6CIT is a brief cognitive screen for dementia (NG97).
whyNot.2: The Mini-Cog is a cognitive screen, not a delirium tool.
whyNot.3: CAM-ICU is for critical care or recovery, not general wards.

A.q: How often does NICE NG97 advise reassessing a person with dementia who is taking an antipsychotic for distress?
options: Every 12 weeks or so
Every 6 months
At least every 6 weeks
At the annual medication review
A.why: NG97 1.7.6: use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and reassess at least every 6 weeks.

whyNot.0: 12 weeks is too long a gap.
whyNot.1: 6 months is far longer than NG97 allows.
whyNot.3: Annual review would leave people on antipsychotics without need being checked.

A.q: Which feature most strongly suggests delirium rather than dementia?
options: Gradual loss of recent memory over 2 years
Word-finding problems for months
Getting lost in familiar places for some months
Sudden onset with fluctuating attention
A.why: Acute onset, a fluctuating course and inattention are the hallmarks of delirium.

whyNot.0: Slow decline over years fits dementia.
whyNot.2: Disorientation in familiar places develops gradually in dementia.

B.q: Mr Patel, 79, with dementia with Lewy bodies, has distressing visual hallucinations. A colleague suggests haloperidol. What is the main concern?
options: Severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions
Haloperidol is less sedating than lorazepam
It may worsen his memory test scores
It interacts with his eye drops
B.why: NG97 1.7.4: in dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia, antipsychotics can worsen motor features and cause severe sensitivity reactions.

whyNot.1: Sedation level is not the key safety concern.
whyNot.2: The serious risk is a sensitivity reaction, not test scores.
whyNot.3: No such interaction is the issue here.

B.q: Mrs Hill, 88, with dementia, calls out repeatedly in the evening. What should the nurse do first under NICE NG97?
options: Ask the doctor for PRN risperidone to settle her
Move her to a quieter ward overnight
Look for causes such as pain or delirium
Ask her daughter to visit less often
B.why: NG97 1.7.1-1.7.2: before any treatment for distress, do a structured assessment for causes such as pain, delirium or inappropriate care, then offer psychosocial and environmental interventions.

whyNot.0: Antipsychotics are not first line for distress.

B.q: Mr Davies, 82, has delirium. He is frightened and pulling at his cannula, and calm talking has not helped. What does NICE CG103 suggest considering next?
options: Regular lorazepam at night for the next month
Short-term haloperidol at the lowest dose
Physical restraint until the delirium settles
Olanzapine for at least 6 weeks
B.why: CG103 1.7.4: if de-escalation is ineffective or inappropriate and the person is distressed or at risk, consider short-term haloperidol (usually 1 week or less), starting low.

whyNot.0: Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and are not the CG103 option here.
whyNot.2: Prolonged restraint is not a treatment.
whyNot.3: CG103 names short-term haloperidol, not prolonged olanzapine.

C.q: Mrs Brown, 77, is referred to the memory service with poor concentration and memory. Over 3 months she has lost interest in her garden, sleeps badly and says she is 'a burden'. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor trial
Book a brain scan before any other assessment
Assess her mood and screen for depression
Reassure her that this is normal ageing
C.why: NG97 asks that reversible causes of cognitive decline, including depression, are investigated before diagnosing dementia; her symptoms suggest depression, so assess mood and risk.

whyNot.0: Dementia drugs are not started without a diagnosis.
whyNot.1: Imaging does not replace assessing a likely depression.
whyNot.3: Loss of interest and feeling a burden are not normal ageing.

C.q: Mr Ali, 86, has dementia and has taken risperidone for 6 weeks for aggression. He is now calm and engaging in activities. What does NICE NG97 advise at this review?
options: Continue indefinitely to prevent any relapse of aggression
Double the dose to secure the benefit
Add a second antipsychotic at night
Consider stopping if no clear ongoing benefit
C.why: NG97 1.7.6-1.7.7: reassess at least every 6 weeks and stop if there is no clear ongoing benefit, after discussion with the person and family.

whyNot.0: Indefinite use contradicts the shortest-possible-time principle.
whyNot.1: There is no reason to increase the dose.
whyNot.2: Adding a second antipsychotic adds risk without indication.

C.q: On the older adults' ward, which plan best reduces the risk of delirium for Mrs Evans, 81, admitted with dementia and a chest infection?
options: Night-time medicine rounds and a bay near the door
Clock and calendar visible, glasses on, sleep protected
Frequent bed moves to the bay with the most staff on shift
Sedation at night to make sure she sleeps
C.why: CG103 1.4.4, 1.4.12 and 1.4.13: reorientation (clock, calendar, lighting), working sensory aids, involving family and protecting sleep reduce delirium risk; 1.4.1 advises against moving people between rooms or wards.

whyNot.0: Medicine rounds should avoid disturbing sleep.
whyNot.2: Moving people between beds or wards increases risk.

reteach.title: Sudden change, think delirium
reteach.question: Why is the quiet patient a worry?

blocks.body: Hyperactive delirium shouts; hypoactive delirium whispers. A withdrawn, sleepy, slow person eating less may be acutely unwell. Compare with their usual self (ask family), do a 4AT, check observations and look for a cause.

blocks.text: 'Settling in' and 'just tired' hide hypoactive delirium.

explain.body: On arrival in hospital or long-term care: age 65 or over, cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture, severe illness (CG103 1.2.1).

test.q: Which is a delirium risk factor listed by NICE CG103 at first presentation?
options: Age 55 years or older
Current hip fracture
Living alone at home
Previous depression
test.why: CG103 1.2.1: age 65 or over, cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture and severe illness.

whyNot.2: Living alone is not one of the four listed factors.
whyNot.3: Past depression is not one of the listed factors.

explain.body: Withdrawal, slow responses, reduced mobility, worse concentration, reduced appetite. Often missed.

test.q: Which change in an 85-year-old inpatient should prompt the nurse to suspect hypoactive delirium?
options: Shouting and pulling at lines
New sleepiness and slow responses
Gradual forgetfulness over a year
Long-standing low mood since bereavement
test.why: CG103 1.3.2: be vigilant for withdrawal, slow responses, reduced movement and appetite, signs of hypoactive delirium.

whyNot.2: Slow decline over a year suggests dementia.
whyNot.3: Long-standing low mood suggests depression or grief.

explain.body: Only for risk of harm or severe distress from agitation, hallucinations or delusions; lowest dose, shortest time; review at least every 6 weeks; caution in Lewy body and Parkinson's disease dementia.

test.q: In which situation does NICE NG97 allow an antipsychotic to be offered to a person with dementia?
options: Wandering around the ward at night
Refusing to take a shower
Repetitive questioning of staff
Delusions causing severe distress
test.why: NG97 1.7.3: only offer antipsychotics if the person is at risk of harming themselves or others, or has agitation, hallucinations or delusions causing severe distress.

whyNot.0: Wandering alone is not an NG97 indication.
whyNot.1: Refusing care calls for psychosocial approaches.
whyNot.2: Repetitive questioning is not an indication.

explain.body: Reorientate; clock, calendar, lighting; glasses and hearing aids; family; protect sleep; treat the cause; de-escalate first. Haloperidol short-term only if needed.

test.q: Which action from NICE CG103 helps a person with delirium most at the bedside?
options: Explaining where they are and who you are
Keeping the lights low throughout the day
Removing their glasses to prevent falls
Limiting family visits to reduce stimulation
test.why: CG103 1.7.2: ensure effective communication and reorientation, explaining where the person is, who they are and your role, with reassurance and family involvement.
